For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "ps ≥ .18", Sentence = "The remaining items showed no evidence of statistically significant misfit (ps ≥ .18) and likewise exhibited small RMSEA values."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: The data collection was in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and received approval from the Institutional Review Board of the FernUniversität in Hagen.
All participants provided informed consent and consent to publish.
The data, R scripts, and supplements can be retrieved from https://osf.io/b4adh/overview?view_only=18e649106da649779926be930b961a6e.
text.formatted: The data, R scripts, and supplements can be retrieved from <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/b4adh/overview?view_only=18e649106da649779926be930b961a6e">https://osf.io/b4adh/overview</ref>.

text.text: People-pleasing is generally understood as a tendency to prioritize others' needs, wishes, and approval over one's own preferences and interests.

Although such behaviors may facilitate interpersonal harmony, excessive people-pleasing has been associated with difficulties in assertiveness, heightened approval seeking, interpersonal dependency, and psychological distress.

Recent theoretical work has further suggested that people-pleasing represents a distinct interpersonal disposition characterized by a strong motivation to avoid interpersonal conflict and maintain social acceptance, even at personal cost.
Consequently, valid assessment of individual differences in people-pleasing is important for both research and applied contexts (Blötner, 2026; Kuang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consequently, valid assessment of individual differences in people-pleasing is important for both research and applied contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kuang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To facilitate empirical investigation of this construct, the People Pleasing Scale was recently developed and validated.

Initial validation studies provided evidence for the threefactor structure (Responsibility, Others' Expectations, Neglect of Own Needs), sufficiently high estimates of reliability, and construct validity using classical test theory (CTT) approaches.
These findings established the People Pleasing Scale as a psychometrically promising instrument for assessing people-pleasing tendencies in adults.
Although the original validation of the People Pleasing Scale yielded promising evidence regarding reliability and construct validity, several important psychometric questions remain unanswered.
In contrast to CTT, item response theory (IRT) enables the evaluation of item discrimination, category thresholds, conditional reliability, and local dependence at the item level.

Therein, item discrimination parameters indicate how effectively an item differentiates between respondents with similar trait levels, whereas threshold parameters identify the levels of the latent trait required to endorse increasingly higher response categories.
In addition, IRT affords the identification of specific regions of the trait continuum at which a measure provides the greatest precision.

These analyses bear implications for score interpretation and refinement of the measure as they can identify particularly informative items and highlight potential redundancies, among others (Embretson & Reise, 2000).
text.formatted: These analyses bear implications for score interpretation and refinement of the measure as they can identify particularly informative items and highlight potential redundancies, among others <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Embretson & Reise, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, an IRT investigation is not simply a replication of previous validation efforts using different statistical techniques.
Rather, IRT provides information that is unavailable within conventional CTT frameworks.

For the People Pleasing Scale, such analyses can clarify whether the scale adequately captures the full spectrum of peoplepleasing tendencies, whether some items contribute disproportionately to measurement precision, and whether all response options contribute meaningful information or whether certain categories are redundant or underutilized.
These issues are directly relevant to the interpretation and application of test scores and therefore constitute an important extension of the original validation research (Embretson & Reise, 2000).
text.formatted: These issues are directly relevant to the interpretation and application of test scores and therefore constitute an important extension of the original validation research <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Embretson & Reise, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Conceptually, people-pleasing may be understood as a broad interpersonal disposition or as a constellation of interrelated but distinguishable facets.
The People Pleasing Scale was developed to capture three theoretically derived dimensions, namely Responsibility, Others' Expectations, and Neglect of Own Needs (Blötner, 2026).
text.formatted: The People Pleasing Scale was developed to capture three theoretically derived dimensions, namely Responsibility, Others' Expectations, and Neglect of Own Needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, these facets are expected to share substantial common variance because they reflect different manifestations of a broader tendency to prioritize others' needs and interpersonal harmony.
Consequently, both unidimensional and multidimensional representations warrant empirical evaluation.
Accordingly, we conducted an IRT-based evaluation of the People Pleasing Scale.

Using a Graded Response Modeling approach (Samejima, 1997), we examined the discrimination and threshold parameters of the items, evaluated model fit and responsecategory functioning, and investigated the measurement precision with which the measure assesses people-pleasing across the latent trait continuum.
text.formatted: Using a Graded Response Modeling approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Samejima, 1997)</ref>, we examined the discrimination and threshold parameters of the items, evaluated model fit and responsecategory functioning, and investigated the measurement precision with which the measure assesses people-pleasing across the latent trait continuum.

text.text: In doing so, the present study aims to provide psychometric information that complements previous validation findings (Blötner, 2026) and advances the understanding of the People Pleasing Scale.
text.formatted: In doing so, the present study aims to provide psychometric information that complements previous validation findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026)</ref> and advances the understanding of the People Pleasing Scale.

text.text: >Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: The present study partially re-analyzed data from the original scale-development project (Blötner, 2026).
text.formatted: The present study partially re-analyzed data from the original scale-development project <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The contribution therefore lies not in providing an independent validation but in generating information unavailable within the CTT framework, such as measurement precision across the latent continuum, category functioning, and potential itemlevel issues.

More specifically, our present research sample is composed of both commercial panel data, specifically the two German samples from Blötner's (2026) studies (Nafter data exclusions = 1,894), as well as an additional data collection conducted at German universities, Ntotal = 2,538.
text.formatted: More specifically, our present research sample is composed of both commercial panel data, specifically the two German samples from <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Blötner's (2026)</ref> studies (Nafter data exclusions = 1,894), as well as an additional data collection conducted at German universities, Ntotal = 2,538.

text.text: As such, our final sample size exceeds the recommended minimum sample size requirements for IRT analyses (n > 500; Jiang et al., 2016).
text.formatted: As such, our final sample size exceeds the recommended minimum sample size requirements for IRT analyses (n > 500; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Jiang et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Our extended data collection involved only the ten-item People Pleasing Scale and questions about demographics.
Across samples, the corresponding items were mandatory to respond to, such that complete data existed for all questions.
From the total sample, 1,918 (76%) participants self-identified as female, 580 (23%) as male, and 40 (1%) self-identified as nonbinary or did not respond.
The mean age was 32.9 years (SD = 12.3, range from 18 to 81).
Most participants (n = 2,328; 92%) reported a high school-equivalent or university degree as the highest obtained qualification.
Moreover, most indicated currently being enrolled as a university student (n = 2,203; 87%).

The comparatively high average age despite the large proportion of university students reflects substantial participation from mature and part-time students as well as the partial inclusion of participants from a commercial panel.
The People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026) assesses Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others' Expectations with three, four, and three items, respectively.
text.formatted: The People Pleasing Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026)</ref> assesses Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others' Expectations with three, four, and three items, respectively.

text.text: Responses were collected on a five-point scale,1 = Does not apply at all,2 = Does not apply,3 = Neutral,4 = Applies,5 = Completely applies.

Blötner (2026) provided initial evidence in favor of the three-factor structure, criterion validity (behavioral economic games), construct validity (concerning benevolent, aversive, and emotion-related personality features), and residual measurement invariance across genders (suggesting that manifest test scores of the People Pleasing Scale can be meaningfully compared between men and women).
In a set of preliminary analyses, we computed response frequencies, means, standard deviations, and skewness parameters for all items of the People Pleasing Scale.
Item response distributions were inspected to identify potential floor or ceiling effects and to evaluate utilization of the five response categories.
All subsequent analyses were conducted in R using the package mirt (Version 1.46.1;
Chalmers, 2012) with expectation-maximization estimation.
We employed the Graded Response Model (Samejima, 1997), which is appropriate for ordered polytomous item responses and estimates both item discrimination and category threshold parameters.
text.formatted: We employed the Graded Response Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Samejima, 1997)</ref>, which is appropriate for ordered polytomous item responses and estimates both item discrimination and category threshold parameters.

text.text: The latent structure of the People Pleasing Scale was evaluated using confirmatory item factor analytic models estimated within the mirt framework.
Besides the three-factor structure reported in the original scale-development study, we also fit a single-factor model.
Model fit was evaluated using the fit statistic M2, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and Comparative Fit Index (CFI).
These indices were used jointly to determine the adequacy of the proposed latent structure.
Moreover, we computed Sample-Size Adjusted Bayesian Information Criteria (SABIC) for both model alternatives, with lower absolute values indicating better fit.
To test the assumption of local independence within the preferred model alternative, we computed Yen's Q3 statistics, that is, item residuals after fitting the model.

Because no universally accepted cutoff exists, we considered both the traditional criterion (|Q3| > .20; Chen & Thissen, 1997) and adjusted criteria that account for characteristics of the instrument and sample (Christensen et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Because no universally accepted cutoff exists, we considered both the traditional criterion (|Q3| > .20; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chen & Thissen, 1997)</ref> and adjusted criteria that account for characteristics of the instrument and sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Christensen et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, Christensen et al. (2017) argued that fixed cutoffs are often inappropriate and recommended evaluating whether the particular Q3s differ by more than .20 from the average Q3.
text.formatted: More specifically, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Christensen et al. (2017)</ref> argued that fixed cutoffs are often inappropriate and recommended evaluating whether the particular Q3s differ by more than .20 from the average Q3.

text.text: Reporting multiple criteria affords a more comprehensive assessment of the extent to which local independence may have been violated.
Item-level model fit was evaluated using the S-χ 2 statistic (Kang & Chen, 2008; Orlando & Thissen, 2000) as well as RMSEA derived from the same model.
text.formatted: Item-level model fit was evaluated using the S-χ 2 statistic <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kang & Chen, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Orlando & Thissen, 2000)</ref> as well as RMSEA derived from the same model.

text.text: Given the large sample size, S-χ 2 values were interpreted cautiously because even trivial deviations from model expectations may achieve significance.
Therefore, conclusions regarding item fit were based primarily on RMSEA values, with S-χ 2 statistics reported for completeness and comparability with previous research.
For each item, discrimination (a) and category threshold (b) parameters were estimated.

Discrimination parameters indicate the degree to which an item differentiates between individuals with different levels of the latent trait, whereas threshold parameters indicate the latent trait levels at which adjacent response categories are equally probable (Embretson & Reise, 2000).

text.text: The functioning of the five response categories was evaluated through inspection of category response curves derived from the graded response models fitted for each subscale because the curves from the unidimensional model are easier to interpret than those from the multidimensional model.
Particular attention was paid to the ordering of threshold parameters and to whether each response category displayed a distinct region of peak probability.
Reliability was evaluated using conditional standard errors of measurement.
Item information functions were additionally inspected to determine the contribution of individual items to measurement precision.
These analyses were used to identify which items contributed most strongly to the reliable measurement of people-pleasing tendencies.

This study investigated the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026) from an item response-theoretical perspective.
text.formatted: This study investigated the People Pleasing Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026</ref>) from an item response-theoretical perspective.

text.text: We did so to expand on the psychometric information about the measure provided by the seminal work that built on evaluations as per the Classical Test Theory.
Most prominently, the original, CTT-based validation study suggested all items functioned similarly, which can be tested by means of applying IRT.
Moreover, the original study treated the scale as uniformly reliable, whereas IRT shows where on the latent trait continuum reliability varies.
Last, unlike IRT, the original validation could not determine which trait levels were required to display specific levels of item endorsement.

Accordingly, we tested whether the People Pleasing Scale accurately discriminates between individuals with similar trait levels (a), which trait levels are required to obtain low, moderate, or high scores on the scale (b1 to b4), and at which regions of the latent trait continua the items and subscale scores provide ample information (i.e., item information and reliability, respectively).
The findings largely support the utility of the People Pleasing Scale, even though certain aspects stand out.
Consistent with previous CTT-based research on the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026), the three-factor IRT model outperformed a unidimensional alternative.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous CTT-based research on the People Pleasing Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026)</ref>, the three-factor IRT model outperformed a unidimensional alternative.

text.text: At the same time, the strong factor correlations suggest that the dimensions share considerable common variance and may reasonably be conceptualized as facets of a broader people-pleasing disposition.
Thus, Responsibility, Others' Expectations, and Neglect of Own Needs constitute distinguishable but closely related manifestations of an overarching construct.

This interpretation is further supported by previous evidence indicating differential relationships within the nomological network with cognitive empathy and extraversion, for instance, despite substantial overlap among the dimensions (Blötner, 2026).
text.formatted: This interpretation is further supported by previous evidence indicating differential relationships within the nomological network with cognitive empathy and extraversion, for instance, despite substantial overlap among the dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blötner, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While the results provided some evidence of local dependence among items, the observed residual associations were weak and limited in scope.
Local dependence often arises from content overlap or common stimulus features (e.g., when items stem from the same subscale).
Such minor violations are not unusual in practice and do not necessarily compromise model validity.
As the magnitude of local dependence was generally small, the assumption of local independence can be regarded as sufficiently met for the present analyses.

Nevertheless, the clustering of elevated residuals among conceptually similar items suggests some degree of item redundancy and may cause slight inflation of discrimination estimates for affected items (Chen & Thissen, 1997; Noventa et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the clustering of elevated residuals among conceptually similar items suggests some degree of item redundancy and may cause slight inflation of discrimination estimates for affected items <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chen & Thissen, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Noventa et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although several items displayed statistically significant S-χ 2 values, the magnitude of model misfit was negligible as evidenced by consistently small RMSEA values.
Given the large sample size, these findings likely reflect minor departures from model expectations rather than meaningful deficiencies in item functioning.
Besides ostensible local dependence in some cases, some items performed poorly in the remaining multidimensional IRT analyses.
More specifically, the third items tapping into
Others' Expectations and Neglect of Own Needs revealed overlapping response categories in the category probability plots, and the third items tapping into Others' Expectations and
Responsibility provided comparatively little measurement information across the continuum.
Instead of limiting the utility of the measure at large, however, these findings suggest promising candidates for future item reduction studies.
Decisions regarding item removal should, however, additionally consider content validity and require independent validation.
The findings also provide an empirical answer to the question posed in the title.

It can be answered by means of the upper threshold parameters b4, which were comparatively low in magnitude (b4, max = 1.63), suggesting that endorsement of the highest response categories does not require extremely high levels of the latent trait.
Thus, endorsement of the highest response categories can occur already at moderately above-average levels of the latent trait.

Despite the size of the utilized sample and the empirical contribution of this study to the assessment of people-pleasing, the present research was not without limitations, especially with respect to the sample.
More specifically, it entailed comparatively young, highly educated, and mostly female university students, primarily enrolled in an undergraduate psychology course.

Thus, the sample may have been somewhat preselected because females and individuals studying social sciences usually report higher scores on benevolent personality traits than males and those studying law, business, and economics (Barbee et al., 1993; Vedel, 2016).
text.formatted: Thus, the sample may have been somewhat preselected because females and individuals studying social sciences usually report higher scores on benevolent personality traits than males and those studying law, business, and economics <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barbee et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Vedel, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Although analyses of differential item functioning of these features may provide valuable information regarding group-specific differences, they were not essential for addressing the central aims of the present study, namely evaluating item-level functioning and measurement precision of the scale as a whole.
Questions concerning differential item functioning across demographic groups represent an important but conceptually separate line of inquiry that should be addressed in dedicated follow-up studies.

Another limitation of the present study is that recruitment took place exclusively in Germany, a relatively individualistic country in which personal goals are often prioritized over those of salient ingroups (Hofstede et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Another limitation of the present study is that recruitment took place exclusively in Germany, a relatively individualistic country in which personal goals are often prioritized over those of salient ingroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hofstede et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the extent to which the present findings generalize to more collectivistic cultural contexts remains unclear.

One might expect individuals in collectivistic cultures to exhibit stronger people-pleasing tendencies, as greater value is placed on social harmony, interpersonal obligations, and attending to the needs of others (Hofstede et al., 2010).
text.formatted: One might expect individuals in collectivistic cultures to exhibit stronger people-pleasing tendencies, as greater value is placed on social harmony, interpersonal obligations, and attending to the needs of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hofstede et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In light of these limitations, replications of the present findings in culturally more diverse samples, along with examinations of differential item functioning across cultural groups, are needed to evaluate the generalizability of our findings.
The findings support the People Pleasing Scale as a psychometrically sound instrument, but refinements are necessary.

Beyond confirming favorable discrimination and reliability, the present study demonstrates that the most extreme response categories can be endorsed at only moderately elevated trait levels and identifies specific targets for future revisions.
These results illustrate the value of item response-theoretical approaches for advancing the measurement of people-pleasing beyond the perspective of classical test theory.
